content: The variability in study designs and the use of different outcome measures have made it challenging to synthesize data and reliably interpret the results. Park (2005) conducted a search for trials up to March 2004 and acknowledged the potential for publication bias. Since then, additional trials have been published, demonstrating that high-quality research in Ayurveda is achievable (Furst 2011). The New Millennium Indian Technology Leadership Initiative, supported by the Government of India, has funded research on Ayurvedic drugs for arthritis. Over the past decade, several Ayurvedic journals have contributed to the growing body of published research in this field. Following the launch of the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) in India, the Department of Health and Family Welfare, along with the AYUSH department, has taken steps to integrate Indian systems of medicine with the NRHM and strengthen national healthcare delivery (MOHFW 2002). The results of trials conducted to date on rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis suggest that while the efficacy data may be modest at best, the safety data from these trials appear more promising. This raises the possibility of integrating Ayurvedic interventions with standard treatments using DMARDs (Chopra 2010). Currently, there is a lack of data on the comparative effects of whole systems Ayurvedic treatments. An updated systematic review using Cochrane methods would be timely and could provide evidence to inform health decisions at national, regional, and global levels for this challenging chronic condition. Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic, progressive, systemic autoimmune inflammatory condition that affects approximately 0.5% to 1% of the adult population in developed countries (Gabriel 2009). The prevalence of rheumatoid arthritis in lowand middle-income countries varies but is generally lower than in developed nations (Dans 1997; Chopra 2001a; Muirden 2005; Joshi 2009). Rheumatoid arthritis is characterized by inflammation of the synovium in flexible joints, leading to joint swelling, stiffness, and tenderness. Over time, this can result in cartilage damage, bone erosions, and joint destruction, which may cause disability, reduced productivity, and increased healthcare costs (Puolakka 2005; Odegard 2008; CDC 2011). The condition predominantly affects women in the perimenopausal age group, with a female-to-male ratio of 3:1. Rheumatoid arthritis is dichotomously characterized by two autoantibodies: rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP). Rheumatoid factor is present (seropositive) in about 70% of individuals with rheumatoid arthritis and is often associated with rheumatoid nodules, more extra-articular complications, and a poorer prognosis in terms of erosive and destructive bone disease and deformities. However, seronegative rheumatoid factor disease can be as disabling as seropositive rheumatoid arthritis in terms of articular deformities. Anti-CCP antibodies are considered more sensitive and specific than rheumatoid factor. They play a central pathogenic role, and seropositivity to both rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies can exist for many years before the onset of rheumatoid arthritis (Sokolove 2014). An association has also been described between tobacco use (including smoking), premature atherosclerosis, and rheumatoid arthritis (Ruiz-Esquide 2012). Although there are ethnic differences in the genotyping characteristics of rheumatoid arthritis polymorphisms worldwide, several studies unequivocally demonstrate the association of rheumatoid arthritis with human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles, particularly HLA DRB1, DR4, and 10 (Scally 2013; Zhou 2013). In approximately 40% of individuals, rheumatoid arthritis can also affect other systems over their lifetime, leading to anemia, vasculitis, kidney disease, diffuse lung inflammation, cardiovascular complications, and eye disorders (Turesson 2003; Myasoedova 2011; Cavagna 2013). People with rheumatoid arthritis also have a higher risk of increased morbidity and mortality due to cardiovascular disease (Gabriel 2009; Meune 2009; Sodergren 2009). The diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis is based on clinical criteria, with laboratory and radiological findings aiding in establishing the diagnosis. The American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism (ACR/EULAR) diagnostic criteria are the most commonly used operational standards for diagnosing rheumatoid arthritis (Arnett 1988; Aletaha 2010). The revised 2010 criteria enable the identification of early disease and the early initiation of aggressive therapy to protect against joint destruction. However, these are classification systems and do not accurately differentiate between rheumatoid arthritis and other conditions in the early stages of disease or those with atypical presentations (Chopra 2011). Conditions equivalent to rheumatoid and musculoskeletal diseases are described in detail in the Charaka Samhita or the Compendium of Charaka (Sharma 1994). There are two schools of thought in Ayurveda regarding the diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis, depending on the preference of Ayurveda practitioners for the diagnostic guidelines in two Ayurvedic texts, Madhava Nidana and Ashtanga Hridaya. Madhava Nidana (a treatise of diagnostic guidelines from the 9th century) describes a clinical condition known as Amavata, which is considered similar to rheumatoid arthritis (Srikantha Murthy 1993). The majority of Ayurveda practitioners consider Amavata to be equivalent to rheumatoid arthritis (MOHFW 2001). Amavata is linked to the gut and is considered the result of the production of ama (a toxic and pro-inflammatory waste product of disturbed metabolism) and vitiated Vata dosha. According to this model, joints and soft tissues are affected by ama, produced in the gut due to weakened agni, food indiscretions, or disturbed dosha equilibrium, resulting in inflammatory and obstructive processes (Srikantha Murthy 1993; Sharma 1994; Chopra 2010). This model of etiopathogenesis is depicted in Figure 1. According to Ayurveda postulates, in general, people with Vata prakriti are more prone to developing joint diseases with severe pain (Srikantha Murthy 1993). Recent investigations utilizing inflammatory and oxidative stress pathway genes have provided evidence that the development of rheumatoid arthritis differs according to prakriti subgroups (Juyal 2012). Events in the pathogenesis of Amavata (the Ayurveda equivalent of rheumatoid arthritis) are based on Acharya 2000 and Chopra 2002a. In Ashtanga Hridaya, another ancient compendium of the Ayurvedic system, the clinical condition considered similar to rheumatoid arthritis is called Vatarakta (Manohar 2014). A smaller proportion of Ayurveda practitioners, particularly those from states in southern India, consider Vatarakta to be equivalent to rheumatoid arthritis, while those who consider Amavata to represent rheumatoid arthritis equate Vatarakta with gouty arthritis (MOHFW 2001). Vatarakta is considered to result from faulty lifestyle and dietary habits that lead to vitiated Rakta and aggravation of Vata, which further aggravates the vitiated Rakta, leading to Vidhana in the blood (similar to inflammation). Vatarakta manifests as the insidious onset of stiffness and inflammation of the joints of the fingers and toes, often symmetrical, sometimes associated with cutaneous manifestations in the prodromal stages, and is characterized by flare-ups and remissions (Manohar 2014). The diagnosis of Amavata or Vatarakta is entirely clinical and depends on the Ayurveda physician's training and experience.
